To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
people’s reports on their characteristics are facilitated by matching them with their relationship partner or in group’s characteristics and inhibited by mismatching them.
people’s reports on the self are facilitated by matches or mismates with their partner’s or in-groups’ perceived characteristics and are inhibited by mismatches or matches, respectively.

(a) people’s reports on their characteristics are facilitated by a match with their relationship partner or in-groups perceived characteristics and are inhibited by a mismatch, and (b) people’s reports of their partner or in-groups characteristics are facilitated or inhibited, respectively, by a match or a mismatch with their own characteristics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how people mentally represent themselves, their relationship partners, and their social groups.
how the self is represented in memory, and how the self is linked to the representations of other people and social groups in memory.
the mental representation of social categories.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the self is represented in the same way as others, and vice versa.
people’s mental representation of the self, in-group, and partner overlap to the extent that they are similar in their perceived characteristics.
the self, other people and social groups are not separate and distinct entities but rather they are constructed in relation to one another.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
people’s self-representations are constructed in relation to their relationship partner’s and in-group’s characteristics.
people have overlapping representations of self and others, and that these representations are constructed on-line.
we are all a little bit like our friends, our friends are a little bit like us, and we are a lot like our best friends.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the self and other people are not separate, independent entities.
people are more likely to make a judgment about themselves when their own characteristics are similar to those of a close relationship partner or a social group to which they belong.
the self, in-group, and partner are all constructed on-line from a common set of mental representations, and the construction process is sensitive to the context in which it is applied.
